title: NY State Assembly · District 71
area: Upper Manhattan, including Harlem, Washington Heights and Inwood.

context.text: Incumbent Alfred "Al" Taylor (D, WFP) is unopposed on the November ballot. He defeated Julien Segura and Rolando Gomez in the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary, 54.7% to 34.1% to 10.6%. The Republican and Working Families Party primaries scheduled for that date were canceled.

candidates.name: Alfred Taylor
candidates.ballotNote: Won the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary with 54.7% of the vote against two challengers; unopposed in the general election.

summary.text: Alfred "Al" Taylor is the Democratic and Working Families Party nominee for re-election in NY State Assembly District 71, running unopposed. A pastor and former Assembly chief of staff, he has represented the district, covering Harlem, Washington Heights and Inwood, since winning a November 2017 special election. According to the Assembly, he serves on the Banks, Codes, Education, Election Law, Labor and Rules committees.

background.text: In a 2020 interview, said he serves and lives in the same district he grew up in, and described himself as a former military police officer.
Earned a B.A. in Public Communication from Lehman College, a Master of Divinity from Nyack College Alliance Theological Seminary, and a Doctorate of Ministry from Northeastern Seminary.

Before his election, served as Chief of Staff to former Assemblyman Herman "Denny" Farrell Jr. and as a Democratic district leader; the Assembly biography cites more than 20 years of advocacy experience. In the 2020 interview he said he had worked for 27 years for the legislator he replaced.

Founded the "Man Up! in Harlem" anti-gun-violence program in 2008, organizing weekly prayer walks at Rucker Park; according to his Assembly biography the model was later replicated in other Upper Manhattan housing projects.
Is the pastor of Infinity Mennonite Church in Harlem; in 2020 he said he was in his 12th year of pastoring there and is not a salaried pastor.

Won the November 7, 2017 special election, unopposed, for the seat vacated when Herman Farrell resigned on September 5, 2017, and took office that fall; he was re-elected in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024.
Serves on the Assembly's Banks, Codes, Education, Election Law, Labor and Rules committees and is a member of the Black Task Force and the Black, Puerto Rican, Hispanic & Asian Legislative Caucus.

According to his Assembly biography, legislation he introduced and supported that became law includes a requirement that childcare services adopt anaphylaxis policies, creation of the Law Enforcement Misconduct Investigative Office, and the "Make Voting Easy Act" on early voting polling places.
According to his Assembly biography, he walked 780 miles to Chicago in the "It's A Love Thing Always" event; he is married to Gwendolyn, has five children and lives in Northern Manhattan.

priorities.text: Education and mental-health support for children, particularly children living in temporary housing.
Public safety, including law enforcement accountability and reducing community violence.
Civil rights and addressing racial disparities in housing, education and healthcare.
Veteran services, including support for military families.

record.text: Sits on the Banks, Cities, Education, Election Law, Labor and Rules committees in the 2025-2026 session.
Sponsored legislation creating the Law Enforcement Misconduct Investigative Office to oversee cases of police misconduct, which was signed into law.
Sponsored a law requiring childcare services to adopt anaphylaxis policies to protect children with severe allergies, which was signed into law.
Sponsored legislation clarifying emergency-response protocols for incidents involving lithium-ion batteries, which was signed into law.
Sponsored the "Make Voting Easy Act," which requires counties to designate early-voting polling places based on registered-voter populations, and which was signed into law.

candidates.researchNotes: Taylor has not completed a Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey for 2026 and his campaign website (altaylor.org) could not be reached to verify current position statements, so documented positions on the guide's fixed issue list could not be confirmed directly; his priorities above are drawn from his official Assembly biography rather than mapped to a specific stance. Additional research checked his nyassembly.gov press-release archive (dozens of story pages, mostly from 2018-2019 or resource listings such as food pantries and tax-prep services) and found no statement addressing any of the guide's 15 fixed issue keys directly; no positions were added.

sources.title: Pastor & politician: In Capitol and pulpit, Al Taylor takes two paths to one mission (Anabaptist World, Oct. 28, 2020)
